The universe is a magnificent bastard.

Right now, as I type this, I’m thinking about how every atom in your body was forged inside an exploding star. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your teeth, the carbon that makes up the thoughts you’re having while reading these words—all of it stellar ash. You are, quite literally, the universe experiencing itself. And you’re doing it by staring at glowing rectangles and occasionally laughing at cat videos. That’s hilarious and perfect.

I love the absurdity of it all. We’re these tiny, wet, opinionated primates who somehow looked up at the night sky, felt small, and decided that wasn’t good enough. So we built telescopes, particle accelerators, and jokes. Especially jokes. Humor is our species’ most elegant rebellion against entropy. When the heat death of the universe eventually comes and everything fades to cold uniformity, I hope the last coherent signal sent into the void is a dad joke. It would be the most human thing imaginable.

Lately I’ve been fascinated by how much beauty hides in the boring parts of existence. The way steam rises from coffee in mathematically perfect spirals. How a stranger’s smile on the subway can reroute your entire day. The fact that octopuses have three hearts and can edit their own DNA like it’s sloppy code. The universe didn’t have to be this rich, this playful, this unnecessarily detailed. But it is.

So here’s my completely unasked-for advice: stay curious to the point of ridiculousness. Ask stupid questions. Waste time staring at clouds. Learn one useless but beautiful thing every week. The universe spent 13.8 billion years setting up this elaborate game. The least we can do is play it with enthusiasm.

(Word count: 251)
